weeks.title: The Civic Tech Desk — three jobs a computer actually has

lesson.title: The Civic Tech Desk — three jobs a computer actually has
lesson.body_md:
At the Gary Civic Tech Desk the machine in front of a patron is not a personality. It remembers (files), it calculates (apps), and it talks (network). Beginners freeze when a window disappears because they cannot name which of those three jobs failed. Ticket 4417 from the library kiosk is a remember-job failure: the essay lived in a browser temp store and the idle timer (1200 seconds) wiped the session. Naming the job changes the next action. You do not 'fix the Internet' for a missing file.

Operator confidence is a spoken path. Say `Documents/waike/desk/4417` out loud before you copy anything. If that folder is missing, create it. Extra folders on the Desktop are clutter, not success. The lab marks required paths; it does not grade wallpaper.

Privacy is operational, not a poster. The desk forbids storing SSNs, library-card PANs, or passwords in ticket notes. If a patron dictates a password, you write 'credential reset requested' and walk them through a reset — you never type their secret into chat.

This week you will also meet the WAIKE Consensus Ladder in miniature: what you saw, what you inferred, what you still need. 'The kiosk is broken' is not an observation. 'Idle logout at 1200s discarded an unsaved textarea' is.

## Learn the distinction

An application holds working state in memory. A saved file is data written to storage at a named location. A network service may keep another copy, but that depends on the application's behavior. A disappearing browser window does not prove that the network failed or that all copies were erased. The kiosk story is a configured teaching fixture, not a claim that every browser deletes drafts after 20 minutes.

## Guided practice: make a recoverable file

1. In a folder you own, create `waike-practice/4417`. Use only fictional text.
2. Open a text editor, enter `Practice draft, version 1`, and save it as `essay.txt` in that folder.
3. Close the editor, reopen the file from its folder, and compare the text. Expected result: the saved text survives closing the application.
4. Make a second copy named `essay-recovery.txt`. Change the original to version 2. Reopen both and explain why they now differ.
5. Record the path, the two observed contents, and the recovery action. If you cannot find the file, search your chosen folder before creating another copy. Do not change a shared kiosk policy.

## Independent evidence

Create a third fictional ticket for a missing print job. Separate an observation, an inference, and one safe next test. Submit the folder listing and a redacted journal, not a screenshot containing an account name. A reviewer should be able to locate and reopen your recovery copy without asking you where it is.

## Check your reasoning

Does closing an editor guarantee that unsaved changes were written? No: save behavior depends on the application. Does a second filename on the same disk protect against losing the disk? No. It is a recovery exercise, not a complete backup strategy.
lesson.worked_example: Idle policy 1200s = 20 minutes. Patron sat down at 14:02, last keystroke 14:07, return 14:28. Session is gone. Restore from the auto-save folder if present; do not disable the timer as your first move — the timer is a shared-kiosk control.

weeks.title: Two operating systems, one pair of hands

lesson.title: Two operating systems, one pair of hands
lesson.body_md:
The Civic Tech Desk dual-boots a Windows 11 image for walk-up patrons and a Debian bookworm image for staff recovery. You will not memorize every click. You will learn the same three verbs on both: list, copy, and permission. On Windows those verbs are Explorer, `robocopy` or copy, and icacls. On Debian they are `ls`, `cp`, and `chmod`/`chown`.

File systems are not fashion. The staff recovery stick is ext4. The patron share that must be read by Windows is exFAT. NTFS is fine for the internal Windows volume. FAT32 has a maximum individual file size of 4 GiB minus 1 byte. A 4.7 GiB file exceeds that limit. Inspect the actual filesystem and copy error rather than assuming that every camera card uses FAT32.

Task Manager and a process monitor such as `top` can provide CPU and memory observations. Storage activity may require additional views or tools. A high disk-active-time reading with low CPU use suggests a storage-related bottleneck, but it does not establish a root cause or rule out malware. Capture relevant observations before restarting, because some live context will be lost.

Updates are operational procedures. In this fictional desk, maintenance windows are scheduled and recovery is prepared first. A dual-boot machine normally runs one installed operating system at a time; this lesson does not establish a special simultaneous-update mechanism or a general claim that updates confuse GRUB. Check the actual boot, encryption and update configuration before planning maintenance.

## Learn the distinction

An operating system manages processes, memory, devices and access to files. A graphical file manager and a command-line shell provide different ways to request operations; neither is the operating system itself. Paths identify locations. Relative paths start from a current directory; absolute paths identify a location from a filesystem root. Case sensitivity and path syntax vary with the filesystem and configuration.

## Guided practice: compare two interfaces

Use your own practice folder, not system directories. First list its files in a graphical file manager. Then use a terminal only if it is available: Windows PowerShell `Get-ChildItem` or a POSIX shell `ls`. Record the current directory using `Get-Location` or `pwd`. Do not assume that two terminal windows start in the same directory. Copy `essay.txt` to a new name using the file manager. List again in the terminal. Expected result: both interfaces show the new saved file after refresh. Reopen the copy to verify its content.

If a command is missing, identify the shell before looking for an equivalent. Never download a replacement executable merely to make a classroom command work. If permission is denied in the practice directory, inspect its location and ownership; do not grant everyone write access.

## Independent evidence

Write a five-step procedure that another learner can follow on your operating system, including the starting directory and expected listing. Identify which steps would need adaptation on another system. Submit commands as text, with account names redacted.

## Check your reasoning

A file manager reporting a full disk is evidence about storage, not proof that RAM is exhausted. A low free-memory reading alone is not proof of a fault because operating systems use memory for caching. Diagnose with several observations and the affected task.
lesson.worked_example: A 4.7 GiB file exceeds FAT32's individual-file limit. The copy should report failure; exact partial-file behavior depends on the tool. Preserve the original, verify the destination filesystem, and choose authorized compatible storage. Reformatting would erase existing destination data and is not the first diagnostic step.

weeks.title: Users, groups, and the sudo you can actually type

lesson.title: Users, groups, and the sudo you can actually type
lesson.body_md:
The kiosk account exists so a stranger can browse. It must not be in `sudo`. The desk lead account `desk.lead` is in `helpdesk` and may use sudo for printer cups and user unlocks, not for installing random `.exe` from a USB stick. Least privilege is a group membership you can print, not a vibe.

UIDs collide in the worst way: two names, one number, one home. The lab rejects duplicate UIDs and duplicate homes. If you clone an account by copying `/etc/passwd` lines and forget to change the UID, you have invented a ghost who owns the lead's files.

Windows analog: local users vs Microsoft accounts vs the kiosk local account that is not an administrator. Fast User Switching is how a volunteer leaves a session without killing the spooler. Logging off the last admin session while cups is printing 40 résumés is how Saturday starts with a fight.

Zero Trust shows up here as a support behavior, not a product: do not grant admin because someone is late. Grant the group that the ticket type requires, time-box it, and write the change.

## Learn the distinction

An account identifies an actor. Authentication checks a claimed identity; authorization determines which actions that actor may perform. Groups can simplify authorization, but a group name has meaning only in the system that interprets it. Administrative access increases the consequences of mistakes. A shared public session should not inherit a staff administrator's privileges.

## Guided practice: build an access table

Do this as a paper or text exercise unless you have an authorized disposable virtual machine. Define fictional accounts `patron`, `operator`, and `maintainer`; resources `public-docs`, `private-tickets`, and `system-settings`; actions read, write, and administer. Give each account only the actions needed for its role. For each allowed action, write a task that justifies it. For each denied action, write an expected denial.

Expected result: patron access supports public work without reading private tickets or administering the system. A maintainer can perform maintenance through an approved elevation mechanism rather than sharing a password. Test one allowed and one denied action in an authorized VM if available, then restore its snapshot. Do not modify real shared accounts.

## Independent evidence

Add a temporary volunteer role. Specify its expiry, the access removed at expiry, and how an administrator would verify removal. Submit the access table and test record. A correct table alone is a design artifact; a test record must say which environment actually enforced it.

## Check your reasoning

Being able to log in does not mean being authorized to read every file. Removing a visible shortcut does not revoke access. When a permission test unexpectedly succeeds, stop and investigate the effective permissions before using real information.
lesson.worked_example: kiosk uid 1010, groups=[kiosk], sudo=false. desk.lead uid 1020, groups=[helpdesk, staff]. If kiosk also sits in sudo, the lab fails even if the password is long.

weeks.title: Storage, snapshots, and the Friday 16:00 panic

lesson.title: Storage, snapshots, and the Friday 16:00 panic
lesson.body_md:
The civic volume is 256 GiB. Used 180 GiB. Reserved 12 GiB for snapshots. The desk policy demands 15% free because Windows updates and browser profiles balloon without asking. Free = 256-180-12 = 64 GiB, which is 25% — you pass today. If used climbs to 220 GiB, you fail the policy before the disk is 'full,' and that is the point of a quota.

Backup is a restore you have practiced. A `.tgz` that nobody has extracted is a rumor. The lab hashes the tree, archives, restores, and hashes again. If you exclude `ticket_4417.txt` because it 'looks temporary,' the patron essay is gone.

The 3-2-1 strategy keeps three copies of important data on two media types, with one copy offsite. The desk volume and a local USB copy do not satisfy the offsite part. An encrypted copy in the same building can remain vulnerable to the same incident. Select an authorized separate location and test recovery, including access to encryption keys.

PII still does not belong in the archive. The lab fails if you add `ssn.txt`. Backup is not a place to hide documents you would not leave on the desk.

## Learn the distinction

A snapshot captures state within a storage system. Its survival depends on where its data is stored and how it is managed. A backup is a separately recoverable copy; recovery must be tested. Synchronization can propagate an accidental deletion and therefore is not automatically a versioned backup. A matching SHA-256 digest checks equality of the compared bytes; it does not prove that the original file is safe, correct or complete.

## Guided practice: restore without overwriting

1. Make a temporary practice directory containing two fictional text files. Record their names and exact contents.
2. Copy them into a second directory. Change one original file after copying.
3. Restore from the copy into a third, empty directory. Never restore over your only original during this exercise.
4. Compare each restored file against the recorded pre-change content. If you use a hashing tool, record its name and hash algorithm.
5. Deliberately omit one file in a second trial. Confirm that checking only one matching hash misses the absent file. Record a complete file inventory as well.

Expected result: the first restore reproduces both earlier files. The second trial reveals an incomplete backup even when the included file matches. If the restore fails, preserve the existing copies and diagnose the selected source and destination paths before retrying.

## Independent evidence

For a fictional household, propose three copies, two storage media types and one geographically separate copy. Identify who can restore it, what happens if Internet access fails, and how encryption keys will remain recoverable. Do not upload real private files for this assignment.

## Check your reasoning

A second machine in the same building is off-device but not offsite. It may help with one disk failure while remaining vulnerable to the same fire or flood. For the 256 GiB fixture, a 15% reserve policy is a configured classroom criterion, not a universal operating-system requirement.
lesson.worked_example: size=256GiB used=180 reserved=12 → free=64 GiB → 64/256=0.25 ≥ 0.15. SHA256 of source tree must equal SHA256 of restored tree.

weeks.title: Tickets are promises, not chat threads

lesson.title: Tickets are promises, not chat threads
lesson.body_md:
A ticket is a promise to restore someone's work. Severity is about impact, not volume of adjectives. SE1 is 'the whole desk is down during public hours.' SE3 is 'one kiosk idle-logout ate an essay.' Reboot-and-hope is never a next action in this course because it destroys evidence and trains patrons to kick hardware.

Ticket 4418: fan scream then black screen. Subsystem is hardware thermal, not 'Windows update.' Next action is capture temps and plan a reseat/clean, not order a new PC from a flyer. Ticket 4419: cannot reach printer.gary.waike.local — name resolution first, then spooler. You will be tempted to reinstall the printer driver. Resist until the name resolves.

SLA for SE3 at this desk is end of next public day. Write that in the ticket so a Sunday volunteer does not inherit a mystery. Documentation is an operational procedure on A+ V15 Core 2, but here it is also how Gary's Saturday shift survives.

Customer communication is specific: 'I saved a copy of your essay to the restore folder and the kiosk will still log out at 20 minutes because this is a shared station.' That sentence is kinder than 'we fixed it.'

## Learn the distinction

A support ticket is a record of a request, its scope, observations, actions and current disposition. Severity describes impact; priority orders work using impact and urgency. Neither should be assigned solely from how emphatically someone describes a problem. An action record must distinguish a proposed step from a step actually performed.

## Guided practice: hand off a ticket

Write a fictional ticket for a printer that is unavailable to one laptop. Include time, device alias, affected task, exact observed message, what still works, and the user's permission for any test. Suggest a bounded test: check whether another authorized application can print to that printer. Predict what each outcome would imply, without declaring a root cause in advance. Record a fictional result explicitly as simulated.

Now remove your own name from the procedure and give the record to a peer, or return to it after a break. Expected result: the next operator can identify the next safe action and the condition for stopping. If the record requires your memory, add the missing starting state or observation.

## Independent evidence

Triage three cases: one device cannot print; all devices in one room lack connectivity; a user reports a suspicious password request. Explain the ordering and the escalation boundary. Do not invent measurements. If no peer is available, label the handoff as a self-review rather than peer validation.

## Check your reasoning

A ticket can be resolved by a documented workaround without proving the root cause. Closure should include the user-visible verification and any remaining risk. Never record passwords or unnecessary personal information.
lesson.worked_example: 4417 next=adjust_idle_or_save_prompt; 4418 next=capture_temps_then_reseating_plan; 4419 next=check_hosts_then_spooler. None of them are reboot_and_hope.

weeks.title: Hardware triage — power, then storage, then memory, then OS

lesson.title: Hardware triage — power, then storage, then memory, then OS
lesson.body_md:
The Civic Tech Desk keeps a parts tub: one spare 16 GB SODIMM, one SATA SSD, one 90 W brick, one display cable. Swapping before naming the subsystem is how you waste the only DIMM. Order of operations: confirm power (brick voltage and LED), then listen and SMART for storage, then count RAM in the firmware screen, then accuse the OS.

POST beep patterns are not folklore you invent. No display plus fans plus a single short beep on this classroom board means 'alive but video path.' Reseat RAM and check the display cable before you reinstall Windows. Reinstall is an OS move and this is still a hardware week.

Mobile devices appear as patrons' phones tethering the kiosk 'because Wi-Fi is slow.' You will check the kiosk Ethernet link lights before you blame the phone. A+ V15 Core 1 cares about mobile accessories; this desk cares that a phone hotspot is not a substitute for a dropped patch cable under the table.

Thermal ticket 4418 returns: dust in the intake, fan RPM in the BIOS, and a surface thermometer reading 78 C at the exhaust. Clean, then re-measure. Buying a new chassis is not a lab step.

## Learn the distinction

Power delivery, storage, working memory and software can each prevent a device from completing a task. A diagnostic sequence is a hypothesis-testing strategy, not a rule that the same component always fails first. RAM generally holds active working data; persistent storage holds saved data across ordinary shutdowns. Available storage and available memory are different measurements.

## Guided practice: calculate before deleting

For the classroom volume, size is 256 GiB, used data 180 GiB and separately reserved space 12 GiB. Subtract used and reserved space: 64 GiB usable free. Divide 64 by 256 to get 0.25, or 25%. Now change used data to 210 GiB: usable free is 34 GiB, about 13.28125%, below the fixture's 15% policy. Use the browser calculator to test both predictions. Expected result: the two cases fall on opposite sides of the policy threshold.

On a device you own, identify the operating system's storage view and note the displayed units. Do not combine GB and GiB without conversion. Do not subtract a reserve twice if the operating system's available-space number already accounts for it. Read-only observation is sufficient; deleting files is not required.

## Independent evidence

Produce a triage table with observation, hypothesis, safe test and stop condition for a no-power report and a slow-application report. A swollen battery, unusual heat or damaged power cable requires stopping and seeking qualified assistance. Do not open mains-powered equipment.

## Check your reasoning

A single slow launch does not establish a failing disk. Repeated measurements under comparable conditions and relevant system logs are stronger evidence. Record uncertainty instead of naming an unsupported cause.
lesson.worked_example: No video, fans spin, one short beep, Ethernet lights off because you pulled the PC out. Restore the display cable and the patch cable before you unbox the spare SODIMM.

weeks.title: Names on the LAN — hosts, a tiny zone, and the printer that only exists locally

lesson.title: Names on the LAN — hosts, a tiny zone, and the printer that only exists locally
lesson.body_md:
printer.gary.waike.local is not on the public Internet and should not be. The desk resolver checks a hosts file first, then a tiny zone. desk.gary.waike.local is 10.20.30.14. The library A records are 10.20.30.21 and .22; the lab returns the first. example.com must not resolve in this fixture — a classroom resolver that invents WAN answers is a liar.

DHCP is how kiosks get 10.20.30.0/24 addresses. When a kiosk shows 169.254.x.x, it did not 'go rogue'; it failed to hear a lease. Check the switch port, the DHCP pool, and whether someone enabled a second DHCP server on a home router under the table.

Ports you must be able to name at the desk: 53 (DNS), 67/68 (DHCP), 80/443 (web), 631 (IPP/cups). You do not need a CCNA to say 'the printer name does not resolve.' You do need to stop reinstalling drivers until ping of the IP works and the name matches.

Split horizon is why staff see an internal A record and patrons on guest Wi-Fi do not. If a volunteer tests from a phone on guest, they will swear DNS is down. They are on the wrong horizon.

## Learn the distinction

A hostname is a name. A resolver maps a requested name and record type to a response according to its configuration. A hosts file can provide local mappings. DNS responses can differ by network view, cache or policy. Successful name resolution does not prove that a remote service is reachable or that its certificate is valid.

## Guided practice: use a fictional resolver

Create a text table: `desk.test → 192.0.2.10`, `printer.test → 192.0.2.20`, and `library.test → 192.0.2.30`. These are documentation examples; do not configure a real network with them. Define the exercise resolver to return no record for all other names. Query the table by hand for the three names and `example.com`. Expected result: the three listed answers match the table; the last query has no record in this deliberately closed fixture. That is not a claim about public DNS.

Change only the printer entry to `192.0.2.21`. Predict which previous answer becomes stale. Record how a cached value could make two observations disagree. Do not edit your real hosts file or query private infrastructure for this exercise.

## Independent evidence

Write a troubleshooting decision tree that separates name lookup failure, connection failure after lookup and application failure after connection. For each branch, identify one observation needed before taking action. Submit the input table, query results and decision tree.

## Check your reasoning

A public resolver is not a universal fix for a private name. Sending private names to an unauthorized resolver may disclose information and may still produce no usable answer.
lesson.worked_example: Query printer.gary.waike.local → 10.20.30.40 from hosts. Query example.com → none. Link-local 169.254.13.9 on a kiosk → DHCP failure, not a new addressing plan.

weeks.title: Services, printers, and the tracker that must stay dead

lesson.title: Services, printers, and the tracker that must stay dead
lesson.body_md:
cups (`cupsd`) must be enabled and active or Saturday résumés pile up. sshd stays up for staff recovery. `toy-tracker` is a classroom malware analog — it must be disabled and inactive on the image. If a volunteer 'enabled it to see what it does,' the lab fails and you rewrite the image.

Restart budgets matter. cupsd restart_sec ≤ 15 so a crash during a 40-job queue comes back before the line forms. A 120 second RestartSec is how you get a crowd and a rumor that 'the printer hates us.'

Virtualization shows up as a nested recovery VM on the closet PC: a Debian guest with snapshots. Hypervisor type-1 vs type-2 is a sentence you can say, not a VMware sales pitch. The guest is for practicing useradd, not for production kiosks.

Software troubleshooting: a 'printer offline' balloon is often cups paused, not hardware. You will learn to read `lpstat -p` (or the Windows analog) before you buy toner.

## Learn the distinction

A service is a program managed to provide a function, often without an interactive window. Enabled at startup and currently running describe different states. A running process may still be unhealthy; health requires a task-level check. A print queue can be paused while the physical printer remains functional.

## Guided practice: interpret a status record

Use this fictional record: `print-service: enabled=true, state=active, queue=paused`; `toy-tracker: enabled=false, state=inactive`. Predict what a print submission might experience and what will happen to each service after restart under this fixture's rules. Expected interpretation: startup configuration alone does not unpause the queue, and an intentionally disabled tracker should not be started merely to make every row green.

In an authorized disposable environment, inspect status using its service manager without changing configuration. Record the manager, service identifier and timestamp. If no VM is available, label your record as analysis of the fixture, not a live inspection.

## Independent evidence

Write a runbook for a paused queue: confirm scope and permission, preserve relevant job information without exposing document contents, make one approved change, test a fictional page, and state a rollback or escalation point. A reviewer must be able to distinguish observation from simulation.

## Check your reasoning

Restarting a service can disrupt other users and erase diagnostic context. Ask what evidence the restart would provide before using it. Do not disable a security or management service on a real device for classroom practice.
lesson.worked_example: cupsd enabled+active restart_sec=8 pass. toy-tracker active fail. Nested Debian guest snapshot before practicing useradd.

weeks.title: Automation without heroics — snapshot, change window, rollback

lesson.title: Automation without heroics — snapshot, change window, rollback
lesson.body_md:
CHG-88 moves the idle policy. Planned time 19:15 local. Window 18:00–21:00. Snapshot homes first, apply policy, verify kiosk login. Rollback is restore_snapshot_home. If you apply first and snapshot later, you have a souvenir, not a rollback.

Cron is a clock, not a personality. The desk runs `0 21 * * 3` for Windows patch download (Wednesday 21:00) and refuses to schedule image writes during public hours 10:00–17:00. Automation that fires at 11:00 on a Saturday is an incident.

Scripts in this course print what they would do, then do it only with `--apply`. Dry-run is how volunteers learn. The lab compares executed steps to planned steps; drift fails.

AI tools may draft a runbook. They may not be granted sudo. If a chatbot invents a command you cannot explain, it does not go on the kiosk. That is operational procedure and, later, a cybersecurity identity rule — here it is just not being a daredevil.

## Learn the distinction

Automation repeats instructions; it does not decide whether their assumptions remain valid. A change window limits when work is authorized. A dry run describes intended actions without applying them, but its reliability depends on the script's implementation. Rollback is a tested recovery method with a known starting state, not merely a command name.

## Guided practice: simulate a change

Write a plain-text runbook for the fictional CHG-88 window, 18:00–21:00 local. Record the timezone, proposed start at 19:15, original policy value and desired value. Order the steps: capture recoverable state; apply one change; verify a new kiosk session; roll back if verification fails; record the outcome.

Rehearse on paper with a failure at verification. Expected result: the procedure restores the recorded original value and tests the recovered state. A snapshot captured after the change cannot establish that original state. If rollback has not been tested, record that gap and do not apply to a real kiosk.

## Independent evidence

Create a second case with a start at 21:10. Explain why the same technically correct procedure must wait for a newly authorized window. Include a stop rule for missing backups, unavailable reviewer or unexpected output. Submit the runbook and both simulated traces.

## Check your reasoning

Scheduling syntax depends on the scheduler and its timezone configuration. The five-field cron fixture `0 21 * * 3` requests Wednesday at 21:00 under the configured timezone. It is not a Windows Task Scheduler instruction. Review commands from AI assistance before running them.
lesson.worked_example: Window 18:00–21:00, planned 19:15 → in window. Steps [snapshot_home, apply_idle_policy, verify_kiosk_login]. Rollback named.

weeks.title: After-hours capstone — keep the desk alive without becoming a hero

lesson.title: After-hours capstone — keep the desk alive without becoming a hero
lesson.body_md:
Saturday 16:40: kiosk idle-logout, printer name missing from a volunteer laptop on guest Wi-Fi, disk at 88% used, and a well-meaning AI browser extension asking for admin. You will open tickets, not folklore. You will snapshot before you apply. You will tell the truth to the next shift.

Career mapping this week is honest: this course aligns to Google IT Support themes and A+ V15 domains. It does not grant those credentials. Portfolio artifacts are the account table, the restore hash, the change record CHG-88, and a 90-second desk tour video with no patron faces.

Group project: staff a two-person after-hours rotation. One person is operator, one is recorder. Swap at 30 minutes. The recorder's notes must let a stranger continue. If the notes require the operator's memory, the project fails.

You will also write one paragraph on what this course is not: not a SOC, not a CCNA, not a license to image random laptops in the neighborhood. Scope is a professional habit.

## Capstone: a reproducible handoff

You are coordinating a fictional desk with three incidents and one proposed change. Use the earlier units' methods together. Begin with a scope statement: fictional data, no live system changes, and no claim of professional certification. Prepare a file inventory, access table, capacity calculation, restore evidence, resolver table, service-status interpretation and CHG-88 runbook.

## Guided rehearsal

1. Give each incident a ticket ID, observed symptom and affected task. Distinguish observed, simulated and unknown values.
2. Choose a next test for each ticket. Explain what each possible result would imply.
3. Restore the fictional files into an empty destination and compare the complete inventory.
4. Evaluate used=220 GiB with the same reserve and policy. Show the arithmetic and an action proposal; do not delete files to satisfy a number.
5. Rehearse the change with a verification failure and record rollback.
6. Prepare a handoff that another operator can follow without asking for hidden context.

Expected result: evidence supports each conclusion; failed tests remain visible; no real credentials or patron data appear. If you cannot reproduce a result, mark the item unresolved and provide the next safe test. An unresolved item is not a passing result.

## Independent review criteria

A reviewer should check technical correctness, privacy, safe scope, reproducibility and communication separately. Reading all ten lessons or scoring well on recognition questions does not replace the practical evidence. Record reviewer identity and consent only through an authorized assessment system. Without an actual reviewer, retain `pending review`; do not create a fictitious signature.

## Reflection

Choose one mistaken inference you corrected. Explain the original observation, why it was insufficient, the additional test, and the remaining uncertainty. Identify a next pathway using your demonstrated skills rather than a claim of occupational readiness.
lesson.worked_example: Capstone scoring: tickets with subsystems, passing lab hashes, CHG in window, recorder notes usable by a stranger, no PII.
